newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Major "furious" with Clarke on Europe.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Major "furious" with Clarke on Europe.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major was reported to be furious with finance minister Kenneth Clarke on Tuesday after remarks by Clarke reopened a chasm over Europe that threatens to split the Conservative Party irreparably.
Senior government sources were quoted by several newspapers as saying Major was "very angry" at Clarke's overt support for a single European Union currency.

Major's Downing Street office said it had no comment on the reports. But senior officials studiously avoided a defence of Clarke's remarks, saying only: "The prime minister has made clear that we have a settled policy which stands."

In another sign that party unity is breaking down over the issue of closer ties with the EU, a junior foreign office minister admonished Clarke, his senior in the government pecking order, saying Clarke's comments had undermined the ruling party's unity.

"I think the difference between Mr Clarke and some of us is that he thinks we can have a single European currency without having a federal Europe. We think... that would be an inevitable step down a road we don't want to advance down," said right-winger Sir Nicholas Bonsor.
"I think he will be out of line with the view of the vast majority of the party and I think it is out of line with what the government policy has been as expressed before."

The government's official policy, which Major instigated to try to bridge the yawning divide between pro-Europeans and so-called Eurosceptics in his party, is that it will decide what is in Britain's interests after the single currency is launched.

In an interview during a weekend meeting of EU finance ministers in Ireland, Chancellor of the Exchequer Clarke said it would be "pathetic" for Britain to wait and see how a European single currency developed before deciding whether to join.

"That would be the worst policy of all, of the British doing their traditional business of not be able to make their minds up and then joining late," said Clarke, seen as the most likely candidate from the Conservative Party's left wing to bid for succession to Major.
Clarke's remarks provoked strong pressure on Major from Eurosceptics to ditch Clarke, the most pro-European member of the cabinet, before a general election due within eight months.

Major negotiated an "opt-out" from monetary union when negotiating the Maastricht treaty in 1991. Eurosceptics want him to rule out entry into a single currency in the life of the next five-year parliament and want that pledge to be a commitment in the Conservatives' election platform.

Getting rid of Clarke would be an extremely risky manoeuvre. Markets, which see him as a "safe pair of hands" and praise his careful management of the current economic upturn, would be dismayed at his sacrifice on the altar of political expediency.

Pro-Europeans would be outraged. They have begun fighting back against the Eurosceptics they fear are dominating political debate. They include senior party figures like former prime minister Edward Heath and a battery of ex-ministers.
The opposition Labour Party is already 20 points ahead in opinion polls. Conservative strategists are worried the European issue will dominate their party conference in early October.
Home Secretary Michael Howard, one of the cabinet's Eurosceptics, heightened speculation over Clarke by carefully sidestepping a request to confirm or deny the rift between Clarke and Major.
"I don't think you should believe everything you read in the newspapers," he said in a BBC interview.
Heath told the BBC the reports of Major's anger were part of an attempt by the Eurosceptics to "stampede" the government into a tougher policy on the single currency.
Heath dismissed suggestions Clarke would quit, saying: "He won't leave the government... (I'm) quite confident because he knows he's done a splendid job and he will keep on doing it."
